# Working with co-authors

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- apply the ICMJE criteria and CRediT to authorship decisions
- keep a multi-author manuscript under version control
- handle author order, disputes, and acknowledgements
:::

Most scientific papers are written by more than one person. The median authorship in clinical medicine exceeded five authors per paper by the early 2020s; papers with twenty or more contributors are standard in large consortia. The benefits — divided labour, complementary expertise, broader networks — are real, and so are the difficulties. Version control failures, absent contributors, disputes over order, and questions of authorship legitimacy are among the most reliable predictors of a troubled submission.

The formal criteria for who qualifies as an author, and the CRediT taxonomy for recording contributions, are covered in Chapter 2 (Authorship and responsibility). This chapter focuses on the practice: keeping the manuscript under control, agreeing on credit before conflict arises, and handling the scenarios that most often go wrong.

## Keeping the manuscript under control

The single most damaging mistake in collaborative writing is losing track of which version is current. Two authors working on divergent copies and then stitching them together produces a document that is worse than either input.

**Use one authoritative source.** Collaborative editors (Google Docs, Overleaf) keep everyone on the same document in real time and make the edit history auditable. If the manuscript lives in Word, name files with date and version (`manuscript_2026-04-19_v07.docx`) and tell co-authors which is current before each editing round. If you write in Quarto or plain text, Git tracks every change: `git diff` shows exactly what changed between drafts, and `git blame` shows who changed it.

**Track changes, then clean.** Circulate drafts with track changes active. When a passage is settled, accept all changes and carry the clean text forward. Never circulate a tracked-changes copy and a clean copy simultaneously — version drift is guaranteed. Agree from the start who has authority to accept changes; usually the corresponding author.

**Explicit deadlines with stated consequences.** *"Comments by Friday 3 May, 12:00 Lisbon time"* is actionable. *"When you have time"* is not. State the deadline, the format you expect (in-document comments, email, or a call), and what happens if the deadline passes. Silence after a stated deadline counts as consent in most collaborative settings.

**Merge by conversation, not by stitching.** When two co-authors give contradictory suggestions on the same passage, resolve the conflict in a fifteen-minute call rather than attempting to honour both in text. Stitched compromises read poorly and reopen the same argument at resubmission.

## Author order

In most biomedical and clinical fields, author order carries meaning: the first author did the primary work and drafted the manuscript; the last author is the senior supervisor or principal investigator; middle authors are listed in descending order of contribution. In some mathematical and physics fields, alphabetical order is conventional. In large consortia, the order may be governed by contribution tier (named authors, writing group, collaborators) specified in the methods.

Agree on order before writing, not after. Revisiting authorship order at submission — when everyone has a clear stake in the outcome — is a reliable source of conflict that is much harder to resolve under time pressure. Document the agreed order in writing, even informally, at the start of the project.

The **corresponding author** manages submission, handles reviewer correspondence, and accepts formal responsibility for the work's integrity on behalf of all authors. This role is often the first author in early-career work; in more senior projects it is often the last. Check the target journal's conventions. The corresponding author signs off on the final submitted version and is the point of contact for post-publication correspondence and corrections.

## CRediT in practice

The CRediT taxonomy (Contributor Roles Taxonomy) lists fourteen standardised roles — Conceptualisation, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review and editing, Visualisation, Supervision, Project administration, Funding acquisition — and requires journals to publish which roles each author performed. Most major journals now require a CRediT statement at submission.

Fill it with all co-authors together, before submission. Two roles that early-career researchers routinely underattribute to themselves: **Writing – original draft** (if you wrote the first draft, this is yours regardless of how heavily it was revised) and **Formal analysis** (if you ran the statistical models, this is yours). Two roles that senior co-authors sometimes overclaim: **Conceptualisation** (did they conceptualise this specific study, or did they approve it after the fact?) and **Writing – review and editing** (does "reviewed the manuscript once before submission" qualify as a contribution that warrants co-authorship at all?).

::: {.column-margin}
CRediT does not define who qualifies as an author — that is still ICMJE's four criteria. CRediT records what each author did. An author who meets only one ICMJE criterion does not become a valid author by holding a CRediT role; conversely, a contributor who holds a CRediT role but does not meet all four ICMJE criteria is an acknowledged contributor, not an author.
:::

## When co-authorship becomes complicated

**The absent co-author.** A contributor who agreed to participate and then stops responding is one of the most common practical problems in academic writing. Address it in writing early, with a clear and final deadline. If they miss it, the question is whether their original contribution still meets ICMJE's fourth criterion — accountability for the work's integrity. Someone who has not approved the final manuscript and cannot be contacted cannot meet that criterion. Consult your institution's authorship policy before removing a co-author; in most cases, this step requires documentation and, where possible, written notice to the person being removed.

**Ghost authorship** — a person who made a substantial qualifying contribution but is not listed — is an integrity violation. Common instances: a medical writer who drafted the manuscript and is buried in the acknowledgements; a statistician who designed and ran the primary analysis and was never added to the author list; a PhD student whose work was published under the supervisor's name. Ghost authorship distorts the scientific record and denies credit to those who earned it. If someone's contribution meets ICMJE criteria, list them as an author.

**Gift authorship** — listing someone who did not contribute enough to qualify — is equally a violation. Common instances: a head of department added as a courtesy; a senior colleague included to improve the paper's reception; an international collaborator who contributed a single email. Journals increasingly require each author to confirm individually that they meet ICMJE criteria; signing off on work you did not genuinely contribute to is a falsification.

**Authorship disputes.** When disagreement cannot be resolved between authors and supervisor, escalate to the institution's research integrity officer or to the journal's editor. Most journals have documented procedures for authorship disputes and will pause review while the matter is investigated. Disputes are harder to resolve after a paper is published and much harder after it has been retracted. Document everything from the start of any project that seems likely to generate disagreement: emails, meeting notes, version histories, and any agreed division of labour.

::: {.column-margin}
The Singapore Statement on Research Integrity and the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity [@allea2023european] both address authorship. Institutions are obligated under these frameworks to investigate authorship complaints. A written record is your protection in any dispute.
:::

## Working with your supervisor

The supervisor-student writing relationship is different from any other co-authorship. In most collaborations, disagreement is symmetrical: each author has standing to argue their position. In the supervisory relationship, the power difference is structural, and both parties know it. This creates failure modes on both sides: the student who never pushes back and learns nothing from the revision; the supervisor who rewrites so thoroughly that the student never has the chance to learn from their own mistakes.

The clearest advice I can give a doctoral student: write the first draft yourself, without asking your supervisor to shape the argument in advance. If the supervisor drafts the introduction "to save time", you have lost the one chance you will have to learn to write an introduction by doing it. You cannot learn to write by revising someone else's first draft. The revision of your own poor draft is where the writing is learned.

When supervisor feedback arrives, distinguish the types of comment. A comment about structure or argument — *"the gap in paragraph three is unclear"* — is scientific feedback. A comment about phrasing — *"I would write this differently"* — may be taste. Both matter, but they carry different weights. Implement structural comments without negotiation unless you have a specific reason to disagree. Question phrasing changes only when they alter scientific meaning.

When the feedback is too vague to act on, ask for specificity. *"I understand this section isn't working — could you point to the specific sentence or argument that's the problem? That would help me revise more accurately."* Supervisors who give vague feedback often do so because they have not had time to read carefully, not because they are withholding the diagnosis.

When two supervisors contradict each other, bring the specific disagreement to both of them together or separately, named clearly. Do not silently implement one and ignore the other; this produces a manuscript with an unresolved internal inconsistency that will resurface at the next round. Most supervisory disagreements about manuscripts are about emphasis and framing, not about facts, and they can be resolved in a short conversation.

When the supervisor returns a manuscript that has been rewritten rather than commented on, read the rewritten version carefully and try to understand why each change was made. The goal is not to preserve your sentences; it is to develop the judgment that produces sentences the supervisor will leave alone.

## Receiving feedback before submission

The peer review chapter covers how to respond to reviewers after a journal receives your manuscript. Before submission, your paper should have been read by at least two people who are not co-authors. Responding to their feedback is a different skill and is worth practising deliberately.

Pre-submission feedback is less formal than reviewer comments. It may arrive as tracked changes, annotated comments, a conversation, or an email. It is also less filtered: a colleague reading a draft may simply say *"I don't understand this paragraph"* without identifying why. This is useful information; it tells you where the reader stopped, even if it does not tell you what stopped them.

Read pre-submission feedback for patterns, not for individual fixes. If one reader flags a paragraph as unclear, it may be the reader. If three readers flag it, the paragraph is unclear. The first task when reading a set of comments is to identify the underlying signal. A single reader's stylistic preference is different from three readers stalling at the same point.

Distinguish the diagnosis from the prescription. A reader who says *"you should cite the 2022 GUIDE-IT trial"* has given you a prescription. The underlying diagnosis is likely *"the comparison with prior work in the discussion is thin"*. The prescription may or may not be right — the cited trial may not be relevant — but the diagnosis usually is. Implement diagnoses. Evaluate prescriptions.

The feedback that stings most on first reading is often the most useful. A comment that feels not like criticism of the work but like criticism of you — *"I don't think this finding is as interesting as you do"* — should be set aside for a day before you respond to it. What feels most unjust in the first hour is sometimes still unjust on reflection, but not as often as it initially seems. The comments that sting are frequently naming something you already know is true and have been avoiding.

## Acknowledgements

The acknowledgements section is for contributors who do not meet authorship criteria: language editors, statisticians who provided a minor consultation, study coordinators, funders (if not in a dedicated funding statement), and patients who participated in the study. It is also currently where most AI-use disclosure resides for tools used in preparation but not in analysis.

Listing someone in the acknowledgements implies that they endorse the work. Many journals require you to confirm that named individuals have given written consent to appear there.

The co-authors you work with shape a scientific career more than most choices you will make. Absent or obstructive ones are a slow, private attrition. Pick carefully, and be the kind of co-author you wish you had.
